content.text: The text reviews historical management of infantile cholera, emphasizing danger, dehydration, feeding, breast milk, clean air, country removal, and cautious medicines. Infants were taken to shaded parks/suburbs, transported by New York’s floating hospital down the bay, or sent to rural New Jersey, Pennsylvania, the Hudson Highlands, upstate New York, or New England. It then describes pseudo-membranous enteritis: chronic mucus-cast discharge, abdominal pain, nervous symptoms, and relapses. Dysentery involves colonic inflammation, tenesmus, mucus, blood, fever or collapse, and possible hepatic abscess; prevention centers on sanitation, clean water, ventilation, and safe food. Treatment historically included rest, milk, irrigation, ipecacuanha, opium, and surgery. Typhlitis, ulcers, hemorrhage, and intestinal obstruction are also discussed, with obstruction requiring urgent diagnosis, restraint from purgatives, opium, irrigation, and timely laparotomy.
